ts-primitives.desc: TypeScript infers types from values. const infers a literal type; let infers a widened one.
ts-primitives.q: What is the difference between type inference and an explicit annotation? When does TypeScript infer the wrong type, so that you must annotate explicitly?
ts-primitives.qsub: What is the difference between let x = 5 (inferred as number) and const x = 5 (inferred as the literal 5)? Why does it matter for unions?
ts-primitives.what:
TypeScript can usually work out types on its own. When you write const x = 5, it already knows this is a number, so you don’t need : number.

There is one subtle difference: with const the type is exactly that value, while with let it is widened to the general type.
ts-primitives.why: The goal of TypeScript is not to annotate everything; less noise means cleaner code. Write types where they act as a contract: function parameters, return types, and exports. Let inference handle local variables.
pros: You write less, because inference does most of the work.
An explicit return type catches mistakes inside the function itself.
as const makes config objects type-safe.
cons: The widening of let can be confusing at first.
Inference sometimes produces a very wide type (for example any[]).
Too many annotations make code noisy.
gotchas: const gives a literal type while let widens it. This difference matters a lot with union types.
Always write a function’s return type. Without it, mistakes surface at the call site instead of inside the function.
An empty array literal like const arr = [] can infer as never[] (or an evolving any array), so write const arr: string[] = [] instead.
terms: TypeScript works out the type of a value automatically, so you don’t have to write it.
With let, the type widens to the general type. For example, "hi" becomes string.
A type that allows exactly one value, such as "hi".
where: Always annotate these. They are the contract other code relies on.
This is where the difference between const and let shows up.
as const locks the whole object into literal types.

type-vs-interface.qsub: Can a type extend an interface? Can an interface extend a type? Show both syntaxes and explain the subtle behavioral differences.
type-vs-interface.what:
In about 90% of cases they behave the same. There are two real differences:

1. type can name anything: a union, a primitive, a tuple. interface can only describe an object shape.
2. Declaring an interface twice with the same name merges the declarations. Declaring a type twice is an error.
type-vs-interface.why: Merging is a feature for library authors, since you can add your own fields to third-party types. In your own code it becomes a bug: you reuse a name in two places and never notice.
pros: interface error messages are slightly clearer.
type can name any kind of type.
Merging lets you extend third-party types.
cons: Accidental merging happens silently, with no warning.
Choosing between the two confuses newcomers for little benefit.
type error messages get very long for large unions.
gotchas: Interview answer: "type can name anything; interface only describes object shapes and supports merging." Everything else is detail.
Accidental merging is a real bug: if you declare interface Config in two places, they silently merge.
An interface can extend a type and vice versa, so the two work together.
terms: A blueprint for an object. Declaring it again merges the declarations.
A name for any type: union, primitive, function, or object.
Interfaces with the same name are combined automatically.
where: Use interface so users can add their own fields.
Use type. You have no other choice.
Either works. Pick one as a team and stay consistent.
type-vs-interface.visualCap: Decide with one question: "Am I only defining an object shape?" If yes, either works. If not, use type.

union-intersection.desc: Union (A | B): the value is one of the two types. Intersection (A & B): the value must satisfy both types at once.
union-intersection.qsub: Sketch the mental Venn diagram. Why does the intersection {a:string} & {a:number} give {a:never} instead of a valid type?
union-intersection.what:
| and & feel like opposites, which is the most common source of confusion.

A | B means the value is A or B, so you can only use what both have: fewer properties.
A & B means the value has the fields of A and B: more properties.
union-intersection.analogy: Union = "tea or coffee". You don’t know which you got, so you can only rely on what both share (it’s hot). Intersection = "coffee and tea together": you get the qualities of both.
union-intersection.why: Unions are how TypeScript models "one of these states can occur": loading / success / error, or different event types. Combined with narrowing (next topic), they let you handle each state safely.
pros: Impossible states cannot be written.
Merging props with an intersection takes one line.
The compiler forces you to handle every case (exhaustive check).
cons: You must narrow a union before using member-specific properties.
Error messages for large unions get very long.
| and & feel backwards at first.
gotchas: A union gives you fewer properties and an intersection gives you more. It feels backwards, but makes sense once you think about it.
The intersection of two different primitives is never, because no value can be both.
Give union members a common literal field (such as status). It makes narrowing much easier.
terms: "Either this or that": one of the two.
"Both this and that": the two combined.
Reducing a union to a single member by applying checks.
where: loading / success / error: three different shapes in one type.
ButtonProps & HTMLAttributes combines your props with the HTML ones.
Different shapes for success and failure.
union-intersection.visualCap: A union value is exactly one of the types (you just don’t know which), so only the shared properties are available. An intersection value has both sets of fields together.

A literal type allows exactly one value. On its own it seems useless, but combined with a union it becomes one of TypeScript’s most useful features.

literal-types.why: With a plain string, a typo goes unnoticed, because "smal" is also a valid string. With a literal union, that mistake is caught as you type, not at runtime.
pros: Typos are caught as you type.
The editor suggests every valid option.

type-narrowing.q: List the ways to narrow a type in TypeScript. What is a type predicate (is), and when do you need one instead of relying on built-in narrowing?
type-narrowing.qsub: What is a discriminated union? How does TypeScript use the literal discriminant to narrow in a switch? What does never tell you at the end of a switch?
type-narrowing.what:
TypeScript reads your if statements. Inside if (typeof x === "string") it knows x is a string, so you can call x.toUpperCase().

This is called control flow analysis, and it is one of the smartest parts of TypeScript.
type-narrowing.why: A union is safe but not very useful on its own: to use a member’s properties, you first need to know which member you have. Narrowing does this without using as. Avoiding as is the real benefit, because as silences the compiler instead of fixing the problem.
pros: You get type safety without using as.
A switch gives you an exhaustive check, so forgetting a new case is impossible.
It works with ordinary JavaScript checks.
cons: Narrowing breaks inside callbacks and async code.
After a function call, TS assumes the value may have changed.
It doesn’t always work with complex conditions.
gotchas: Narrowing breaks inside callbacks, because TS can’t know when they will run. Copy the value into a local const first.
typeof null === "object", so check x === null first.

TypeScript works out the type by reading your if statements.

where: Model success and error with a discriminated union.

nullability.desc: With strictNullChecks on, null and undefined are distinct types that you must handle explicitly. The non-null assertion (!) removes them, unsafely.
nullability.q: What changes when you enable strictNullChecks? Explain the non-null assertion operator (!) and when it is a code smell versus genuinely necessary.
nullability.qsub: What is the difference between an optional property a?: string (string | undefined) and a: string | null? When does it matter?
nullability.what:
Without strictNullChecks, null hides in every type: string effectively means "string or null", and TypeScript can’t protect you.

With it on, null and undefined are separate types, and you can’t proceed without handling them.
nullability.why: "Cannot read properties of undefined" is the most common JavaScript crash. strictNullChecks catches that whole class of bugs before the code runs, with a single flag. It is the most valuable TypeScript flag, so keep strict: true on.
pros: The most common JavaScript crash is caught before the code runs.
Handling with ?. and ?? stays concise.
The types show what might be missing.

People silence errors with !, which defeats the whole point.
Sometimes you must add a check even when you know the value exists.

x?: number and x: number | undefined are different: with the former, the field can be missing entirely.
When migrating an old project, enable it file by file rather than all at once.

"Trust me, this isn’t null." The compiler stays quiet.
The field may or may not exist.

enums.desc: Regular enums generate a runtime JS object. const enums are erased at compile time (inlined). String literal unions are the modern, zero-runtime alternative.
enums.q: What is the difference between a regular enum, a const enum, and a string literal union? Why do many teams prefer unions over enums?
enums.qsub: What is the problem with const enum across module boundaries? Why does isolatedModules forbid const enums from external modules?
enums.what:
enum feels like a natural TypeScript feature, but it is one of the few constructs that generates real JavaScript at runtime. The rest of the type system disappears after compilation; enums don’t.

In most cases a simple literal union does the job better.
enums.why:
Enums have three hidden drawbacks: they add extra code to the bundle, numeric enums are only loosely type-safe (arbitrary numbers can be assigned), and they are TypeScript-only, so they behave oddly when consumed from plain JavaScript.

Today’s advice is to default to a union and use an enum only when you truly need reverse mapping.

String enums are readable when debugging.
Reverse mapping (number to name) is only available with enums.
cons: Numeric enums are loosely typed: arbitrary numbers can be assigned.
They add real code to the bundle, while a union costs nothing.
const enum breaks with modern bundlers (Vite/esbuild).
gotchas: With a numeric enum, any plain number value is assignable, and before TS 5.0 even let s: Size = 99 passed. If you must use an enum, choose a string enum.
const enum breaks under isolatedModules. If you use Vite or esbuild, avoid it entirely.
Interview answer: "Default to a union: zero runtime cost and full type safety. Use an enum only for reverse mapping."
terms: A group of named constants. It creates a real object at runtime.
The same, but values are inlined at compile time.
"a" | "b" is often a better alternative to an enum.
where: A literal union should be the default.
When you need a name from a number, use an enum.
Existing enums are fine; there’s no need to change them. Just use unions in new code.

structural-typing.what: TypeScript doesn’t care about a type’s name; it checks whether the shape matches. If an object has the required fields, it counts as that type, even if it has never heard of the interface.
structural-typing.analogy: Duck typing: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." The name doesn’t matter, only the behavior.
structural-typing.why: This means you can pass third-party objects to your functions without modifying them. The drawback is that UserId and PostId are both string, so TypeScript treats them as the same thing and won’t catch a wrong id. (The remedy is “branded types.”)
pros: Flexible: objects don’t need to declare that they implement an interface.
Works smoothly with third-party code.
Mock objects for tests are easy to create.
cons: Different things with the same shape become interchangeable (UserId vs PostId).
The excess property check rules seem odd at first.
You have to improvise (branding) to get nominal typing.
gotchas: The excess property check applies only to object literals. It doesn’t apply when you assign from a variable, and that confuses a lot of people.
Because typing is structural, UserId and PostId (both strings) are the same type, which is how real ID mix-up bugs happen.
In an interview, say “TypeScript is structural, not nominal” and also mention a drawback. That makes your answer stand out.
terms: Types match based on shape, not name.
Types match based on name, as in Java or C#. TypeScript doesn’t work this way.

keyof-typeof.desc: keyof T yields a union of the known public property names of T. typeof gives you the type of a value at the type level, which is essential for deriving types from values.
keyof-typeof.what:
Two small operators that together form one of the most common TypeScript patterns.

keyof T is the union of all keys of T. typeof x is the type of the value x. Combined, they give you "the type of this object's keys".
keyof-typeof.why: Without them, you write keys out by hand, and the day you add a key to the object, the type goes stale without anyone noticing. With keyof typeof, the type always stays in sync with the object.
pros: The type always stays in sync with the object.
No need to write keys by hand.
The return types of generic functions become exact.
cons: typeof has two meanings (JavaScript and TypeScript), which causes confusion.
keyof also includes optional and readonly keys.
Nested objects need long chains.
gotchas: In a type position, typeof means the TypeScript operator; in a value position it means the JavaScript one. Same word, two worlds.
keyof typeof OBJ is a pattern worth memorizing. You will use it daily.
keyof always sees the keys, but values widen unless the object is as const, which matters if you also derive value types.

Extracts the type of a value (in the type system).

indexed-access.desc: T[K] gives the type at key K inside T. It supports nested access, union keys, and extends keyof constraints, enabling type-safe property lookups.
indexed-access.qsub: What happens when K is not a valid key of T? How do you constrain K at the type level? What is the difference between T[string] and T[keyof T]?
indexed-access.what:
Just as user.name reads a value, User["name"] reads a type.

For arrays, T[number] means "whatever is inside this array."
indexed-access.why: Re-writing a type is a common source of bugs: the original changes and the copy goes stale. With indexed access you extract a type instead of rewriting it, so it updates automatically.
pros: Eliminates type duplication completely.
When the original changes, the extracted type updates automatically.
Extracting types from config arrays takes one line.

assertion-fns.desc: Functions that throw when a condition fails and tell the compiler to narrow the type (asserts x is T). Added in TypeScript 3.7. Cleaner than an if-then-throw pattern.

It’s an if for types. Read it as: "if A fits into B, then X, otherwise Y."

All the built-in utility types are built from it, and they make sense once you understand it.
With infer you can extract parts of a type.
cons: Nested conditionals are hard to read quickly.
Distribution over unions can be surprising.
Error messages can be nearly incomprehensible.

mapped-types.what:
Just as array.map() loops over each item, a mapped type loops over each key and builds a new type.

An abstract class is deliberately incomplete. Some of its methods are fully implemented (shared by every subclass) and some are abstract, which each subclass must implement itself.

So the rule is: shared code means abstract class; just a contract means interface.

If a subclass forgets something, it is caught at compile time.
It can also be used as a type.

Deep hierarchies get heavy quickly.
In JavaScript, composition is often a better fit.

A small set of utilities for working with this.

Honestly: ThisType is rarely needed today. It was built for Vue 2-style APIs that rely on this. But it does come up in interviews.
this-type-util.why: In Vue 2 you wrote methods: { greet() { this.name } }, and this had to reach into data. ThisType let a library author make that type-safe.

The this parameter is genuinely useful in DOM handlers.

They make template literal types useful.
They distribute over unions automatically.

You cannot create your own intrinsics.
Other string operations use recursive types, which are slow.

tsconfig.what:
A file that controls how strict TypeScript is, which files it checks, and what the output looks like.

It has over 100 options, but only 8-10 really matter. The defaults for the rest are fine.
tsconfig.why: Most complaints that "TypeScript didn’t save me" come from a bad config, usually strict being off. Changing that one line gives you back half of TypeScript’s value.

skipLibCheck makes builds much faster.
Use extends to share settings across a monorepo.
cons: 100+ options are intimidating for newcomers.
You have to configure paths separately in the bundler.
A wrong target/lib causes strange errors.

"strict": true is a shortcut that turns on 8 separate flags. Each catches its own kind of mistake.

Of these, strictNullChecks alone delivers about half of TypeScript's benefit.

strictNullChecks alone prevents the most common JS crash.
useUnknownInCatchVariables makes catch blocks safe.
cons: An old codebase can show hundreds of errors at once.
strictPropertyInitialization clashes with how many classes are written.
Teams silence errors with ! and any, which hides real issues.

When migrating an old project, turn strict on, add // @ts-nocheck to each failing file, then remove them one by one.

The flag that delivers the most benefit.
where: Enable it on day one. Adding it later is ten times harder.

declaration-files.q: What is a .d.ts file? When do you write one yourself, and when do you install @types/*? What is the difference between declare module and declare global?
declaration-files.qsub: How does TypeScript resolve types for an npm package? In what order does it check the exports map? What is skipLibCheck, and when does it become a trap?
declaration-files.what:
A .d.ts file contains only types and no executable code. Its job is to describe the shape of JavaScript code that has no types of its own.

You will meet them in three places: shipped inside a library, in a @types/* package, or in your own project.
declaration-files.why: Many older JavaScript libraries ship without types. A .d.ts file lets you add them without touching the library. And if you publish a library yourself, declaration: true generates them for you.
pros: You get types without changing the library.
With declaration: true, your library's types are generated automatically.
Module augmentation lets you extend third-party types.
cons: Nothing verifies a .d.ts file against the real code, so a wrong declaration silently lies.
@types packages can lag behind the library version.
Global declarations affect the entire project.
gotchas: .d.ts is a promise, not a guarantee. You can write a wrong type and the compiler will accept it, so the bug only shows up at runtime.
Every Vite/Webpack project needs declare module "*.svg", otherwise asset imports fail to type-check.
declare global only works inside a module file (one that contains an import or export).

"This thing exists elsewhere, and this is its type."

In TypeScript, module handling depends on three settings working together: module, moduleResolution, and the package.json "type" field.

Most "Cannot find module" errors happen because these three do not agree with each other.

pros: Builds are much faster because only the changed part is rebuilt.
The compiler enforces package boundaries.
The editor gets faster too.

compiler-api.qsub: What is an AST in TypeScript? What is the difference between ts.Node, ts.Type, and ts.Symbol? How do tools like ts-morph simplify working with the AST?
compiler-api.what:
TypeScript is not just a compiler. It is also a library: you can import it, parse code, walk the syntax tree, and generate new code.

The raw API is heavy, so for most work use ts-morph, a friendlier wrapper around it.
compiler-api.why: Codemods (changing a pattern across a whole codebase), custom lint rules and code generation are all built on this. If you worked through the RAG journal, the chunking with ts-morph used exactly this.

Access to type information, which regex can never give you.
Easy to learn through ts-morph.

lib-target.desc: target sets the JS language level (ES2015, ES2020, ESNext). lib selects which built-in type declarations are included. module sets the output module system. The three interact.
lib-target.q: How do target, lib, and module interact in tsconfig? Why would you set target: ES2015 but lib: ES2023? What does "lib" actually control?
lib-target.qsub: Why does using Array.from in source NOT cause a compile error with target: ES2015 (hint: lib)? What is the difference between lib and @types? When should you use --skipLibCheck?
lib-target.what:
These settings are interrelated, which is why they confuse people:

target = "which JS version the output is written in".
lib = "which built-in types are visible to my code".

Setting target also sets a default lib, but you can override it.
lib-target.why: A wrong target causes problems either way. Too old, and # private fields compile into slow WeakMap code. Too new, and the output crashes in older browsers. A wrong lib makes things like document show up as "not found".

With lib, APIs your runtime lacks don't show up at all.
With types, you control which type packages from node_modules are included.
cons: The relationship between lib and target is confusing.
A newer lib means you must add polyfills yourself.
Errors from a wrong setup are hard to decipher.

discriminated-unions.desc: A union of types that share a literal discriminant field. TypeScript narrows each branch of a switch, and assigning the leftover value to never enforces exhaustiveness.
discriminated-unions.qsub: What is the never type, conceptually? How does assigning an unhandled case to a never variable enforce exhaustiveness at compile time?
discriminated-unions.what:
A union where every member has a common field with a distinct literal value, such as status, kind or type.

Once you check that field, TypeScript knows the full shape of the remaining properties.
discriminated-unions.why: This is TypeScript's most useful pattern. It makes "impossible states" unrepresentable: loading: true can never coexist with data. And when you add a new case, the compiler points out every place that needs updating.

Narrowing is automatic, so you don't need as.
Exhaustive checking means you can't forget a new case.

Every member must carry the discriminant field.
Error messages for large unions can get long.

Always add the exhaustive check, like const _never: never = s, so a missing case becomes a compile error.

Making the compiler confirm that no case was left out.
A type that can never hold a value.

ts-decorator-composition.q: How do decorators compose? In what order do multiple decorators on one method run?
ts-decorator-composition.qsub: How does NestJS use decorators to define routes? What is the difference between the @Controller and @Injectable decorators?
ts-decorator-composition.what:
Definition: Composition means applying several decorators to the same method or class. There are two different orders, and it's a favorite interview question:

  • Apply order is bottom-up: the lowest decorator wraps first.
  • Execution order at call time is top-down: the topmost decorator is the outermost layer.

Factories add a third order: in @log(1) @log(2), the factory calls happen top-down, and then the resulting decorators apply bottom-up.
ts-decorator-composition.analogy: Onion layers. Wrapping (apply) goes from the inside out; cutting (call) hits the outer layer first.
ts-decorator-composition.why: Get the order wrong and the bug can go unnoticed: with @cache @auth, the cache runs first, so an unauthorized user could receive a cached result! @auth @cache is correct: check auth first, then the cache.
pros: Build small, focused decorators and combine them
Each concern lives in its own layer, which keeps responsibilities separate
Changing the order changes the behavior, so you control it explicitly
cons: An ordering bug is completely silent
Past 3+ layers, debugging gets painful
Each layer shows up as a frame in the stack trace
gotchas: Apply is bottom-up but execution is top-down. They are reversed, and interviewers ask about it.
Always put @auth above @cache, or a cached response could be served without an auth check
Factory calls (the ones with arguments) happen first, top to bottom: a third distinct order
